abstract:
Ferritin-guided iron supplementation in whole blood donors: optimal dosage, donor response, return and efficacy (FORTE)—a randomised controlled trial protocol

2022-03-01417

…

|OA|1|Research category|[1] Biomedical and Clinical Sciences [2] Nutrition and Dietetics|
Research Direction:iron supplementation effects ｜ donor iron status assessment ｜ optimal iron dosage determination

Introduction
Regular whole blood donors are at risk of iron deficiency without anemia due to Hb-bound iron loss during donation. Reduced ferritin levels are common among frequent donors and are associated with various symptoms. While Hb levels are measured before donation, they don't reflect iron stores. Ferritin measurements are becoming more common, and donor deferral based on low ferritin levels can demoralize donors and reduce return rates.
Oral iron supplementation can reduce recovery time, but the optimal intake frequency and dosage are unknown, as are the influences of dietary status and treatment adherence. This study aims to determine the effect of iron supplementation on various parameters in whole blood donors with low ferritin levels by comparing different intake frequencies and dosages.

Strengths and limitations of this study
This is a large, double-blind, randomized controlled trial to determine the optimal iron supplementation protocol. Outcome variables include ferritin and hemoglobin levels, symptoms, and side effects. Participants are thoroughly characterized at baseline. A limitation is the limited number of follow-up visits, though the time points are relevant and temporal patterns are modeled based on earlier studies.
Methods and analysis
The study is conducted at Sanquin Blood Bank. Eligible donors are invited to participate, and those with baseline ferritin levels ≤30 μg/L are randomly allocated to one of six trial arms varying in intake frequency and dosage. Follow-up visits occur at 56, 122, and 182 days. Data are collected through questionnaires and blood samples.
The trial uses ferrous bisglycinate iron supplements, and participant randomization is done using a block randomisation method. Data analysis includes descriptive statistics and multiple regression models, and potential effect modifiers and confounders are examined. Study monitoring is performed by the TAPAS Group, and focus group interviews are conducted to gather opinions on iron supplementation.
Experiment

Donors are recruited, and their eligibility is assessed. Baseline measurements and questionnaires are taken, and those with appropriate ferritin levels are randomized and receive supplements. Follow-up visits involve blood sample collection and questionnaire completion. The MedApp is used to assist with compliance. Samples are analyzed for ferritin and complete blood count, and DNA is isolated for later use. Additional samples are stored for potential post-study measurements.
Results

Descriptive statistics will be presented for different groups. The multiple regression model will be used to analyze primary study parameters if assumptions are met. Potential effect modification and confounding will be examined, and variables will be added to models as needed.

Discussion
The study's findings will be discussed in the context of previous research. The implications of the results for iron supplementation in whole blood donors will be explored, including the effects on iron deficiency-related symptoms, donor return rates, and the role of different dosages and intake frequencies. The limitations of the study, such as the limited follow-up visits, will also be considered, and suggestions for future research will be provided.

##
AbstractBackground Frequent whole blood donors have an increased risk of developing iron deficiency. Iron deficiency can have detrimental health effects when left untreated. Donation intervals are commonly too short to replenish iron stores and extending these reduces donor availability. Oral iron supplementation is known to shorten iron store recovery time but may also induce gastrointestinal complaints. We aim to optimise the effectiveness of iron supplements while minimising the risks of side effects.
Therefore, we will evaluate the impact of different iron supplementation protocols in terms of dosage and frequency on ferritin and haemoglobin levels, gastrointestinal side effects, iron deficiency-related symptoms and donor return compared with placebo supplementation. Methods Twelve hundred whole blood donors with ferritin levels ≤30 μg/L are included into a double-blind, randomised controlled trial.
Participants are randomly allocated to one of six arms, administering capsules containing 0 mg, 30 mg or 60 mg of iron, either on alternate days or daily for 56 days. At baseline and 56, 122 and 182 days of follow-up, ferritin and haemoglobin levels are measured, and compliance, donor return, dietary iron intake, gastrointestinal, iron deficiency-related symptoms and general health are assessed by questionnaire.
Ethics and dissemination This study will provide a comprehensive overview of the effects of different frequencies and dosages of administration of iron supplements on iron status and health effects, thereby considering individual differences in treatment adherence and lifestyle. The outcome will provide scientific evidence to guide the debate if and how oral iron supplements may support the recovery of whole blood donors with low ferritin levels. Trial registration number NL8590; The Dutch trial registry.
